line: e4 e6 d4 d5 e5 b6 c3 Qd7
teaches: A plan to trade off your worst piece can fail on a single check. Before playing the trade, look at the square the enemy queen would check from once the recapture lands — if a knight or rook would hang to it, spend one move covering that square first. The preparation move looks slow and is the difference between a good plan and a lost piece.
explains: The queen steps to d7 taking a4 in hand and holding the bishop on c8 that is about to travel. Trading immediately would have invited a check on that very square, forking king and the piece that recaptured.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 e5 b6 c3 Qd7 Bd3 Ba6 Ne2
teaches: Where a knight goes should be decided by which PAWN you intend to advance later. The natural central square sits in front of the f-pawn and quietly cancels the plan of pushing it; the square beside it does the same defensive work and leaves the pawn free to charge. Decide the plan first, then pick the developing square that serves it.
explains: The knight comes to e2 holding d4 and c3 and covering f4, with the f-pawn unobstructed behind it. Once the king is castled, that pawn can run at the base of the enemy chain.
